idiom_name: package-level New / NewX constructor functions returning *T or (T, error)
implementation_notes: Go has no constructors, so a constructor is simply a function that makes new instances: the convention is New or NewTypeName returning the type, or the interface when the concrete type is uninteresting - Effective Go states the constructor should return an interface value in that case (crc32.NewIEEE returns hash.Hash32). Return the concrete *T by default (accept interfaces, return structs), return (*T, error) when construction can fail, and put defaults and validation inside the function; because a well-designed Go type often has a usable zero value, the honest form of the pattern is 'no constructor at all' unless validation, defaults or subtype choice are actually required.
pitfalls: The typed-nil trap: returning a nil *T through an interface return type yields a non-nil interface that passes == nil checks and panics on the first method call - return an untyped nil on the error path or return concrete types.
A New function that can fail must return an error rather than panic or hand back a half-built *T; callers must never read the value when err != nil.

If the struct's invariant-carrying fields are exported, callers bypass the constructor with a composite literal and build invalid values - keep those fields unexported when New is what enforces the rule.
